claim: Slow waves and cognitive output have been modulated in humans by phase-targeted auditory stimulation.
source: Slow waves and cognitive output have been modulated in humans by phase-targeted auditory stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about human studies.

claim: This study reports the successful employment of slow waves' phase-targeted closed-loop auditory stimulation (CLAS) in rats.
source: Here, we report the successful employment of slow waves' phase-targeted closed-loop auditory stimulation (CLAS) in rats.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a primary finding of the study.

claim: CLAS specifically altered delta (slow waves) and sigma (sleep spindles) power persistently over chronic periods of stimulation without affecting 24 hr sleep-wake behavior.
source: Without affecting 24 hr sleep-wake behavior, CLAS specifically altered delta (slow waves) and sigma (sleep spindles) power persistently over chronic periods of stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Up-phase CLAS does not elicit a significant change in behavioral performance.
source: While up-phase CLAS does not elicit a significant change in behavioral performance, down-phase CLAS exerted a detrimental effect on overall engagement and success rate in the behavioral test.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 7.

claim: Down-phase CLAS exerted a detrimental effect on overall engagement and success rate in the behavioral test.
source: While up-phase CLAS does not elicit a significant change in behavioral performance, down-phase CLAS exerted a detrimental effect on overall engagement and success rate in the behavioral test.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 7.

claim: Overall CLAS-dependent spectral changes were positively correlated with learning performance.
source: Overall CLAS-dependent spectral changes were positively correlated with learning performance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by correlation data in Figure 9.

claim: Phase-targeted CLAS of slow waves in rodents is efficient, safe, and stable over chronic experimental periods.
source: Altogether, our results provide proof-of-principle evidence that phase-targeted CLAS of slow waves in rodents is efficient, safe, and stable over chronic experimental periods, enabling the use of this high-specificity tool for basic and preclinical translational sleep research.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental results.

claim: Modulation of slow wave sleep (SWS) has increasingly gained attention over recent years.
source: In particular, modulation of slow wave sleep (SWS) has increasingly gained attention over recent years.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background context.

claim: Tailoring novel stimulation tools to effectively optimize SWS profiles appears crucial to intervene SWS-related cognition.
source: Tailoring novel stimulation tools to effectively optimize SWS profiles appears crucial to intervene SWS-related cognition (Mander et al., 2013; Papalambros et al., 2017), as well as other important brain and body processes, in both rodents and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Auditory stimulation during SWS was successfully implemented in human subjects in laboratory-based settings.
source: More recently, auditory stimulation during SWS was successfully implemented in human subjects in laboratory-based settings.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: Targeting ongoing slow waves in their up-phase enhanced slow oscillations during SWS, while targeting the waves' down-phase had the opposite effect.
source: Targeting ongoing slow waves in their up-phase enhanced slow oscillations during SWS, while targeting the waves' down-phase had the opposite effect.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from previous human studies.

claim: SWS is characterized by brain slow oscillatory activity in the delta-frequency range (0.5–4 Hz) and oscillations <1 Hz among its most distinctive features in the human electroencephalogram (EEG).
source: Memory formation is one of the most intriguing sleep-dependent brain processes for which the links between SWS—characterized by brain slow oscillatory activity in the delta-frequency range (0.5–4 Hz) and oscillations <1 Hz among its most distinctive features in the human electroencephalogram (EEG) (Timofeev, 2011)—and motor learning (Fischer et al., 2002; Stickgold, 2005; Walker et al., 2002), synaptic downscaling (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014), and consolidation mechanisms (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Rasch and Born, 2013) have been exhaustively studied.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Ngo and colleagues found enhanced performance during a paired-associates learning task in subjects undergoing up-phase auditory stimulation.
source: Initially, Ngo and colleagues found enhanced performance during a paired-associates learning task in subjects undergoing up-phase auditory stimulation (Ngo et al., 2013a), and soon several other studies employing similar stimulation paradigms replicated the enhanced memory effect, although with more modest effect sizes (Leminen et al., 2017; Ong et al., 2016; Papalambros et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Auditory disruption of slow waves perturbing local SWS in the motor cortex attenuated the brain's SWS-dependent capacity to undergo neuroplastic changes.
source: In a novel implementation of this concept, some of us found that auditory disruption of slow waves perturbing local SWS in the motor cortex attenuated the brain's SWS-dependent capacity to undergo neuroplastic changes (Fattinger et al., 2017), corroborating that SWS integrity is critical to maintain cognitive efficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Some authors proposed that enhancing slow waves and spindles by auditory stimulation was insufficient to improve memory above sham.
source: However, some authors proposed that enhancing slow waves and spindles by auditory stimulation was insufficient to improve memory above sham (Cox et al., 2014; Ngo et al., 2019; Weigenand et al., 2016), suggesting that the effects of auditory stimulation on memory are moderate and highly variable inter- and intra-studies, and evidencing that a better understanding of the method is needed.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The effects of auditory stimulation on memory are moderate and highly variable inter- and intra-studies.
source: However, some authors proposed that enhancing slow waves and spindles by auditory stimulation was insufficient to improve memory above sham (Cox et al., 2014; Ngo et al., 2019; Weigenand et al., 2016), suggesting that the effects of auditory stimulation on memory are moderate and highly variable inter- and intra-studies, and evidencing that a better understanding of the method is needed.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from cited studies.

claim: Online NREM sleep staging had a mean sensitivity of 12%, indicating how strictly the staging tool identifies sustained NREM sleep.
source: Overall, online NREM sleep staging had a mean sensitivity of 12%, indicating how strictly the staging tool identifies sustained NREM sleep, and specificity of 98%, highlighting the high rejection rate of events in disagreement with NREM characteristics (Figure 3a, see detailed methods 'EEG/EMG offline scoring and online staging validation' section).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: Online NREM sleep staging had a specificity of 98%, highlighting the high rejection rate of events in disagreement with NREM characteristics.
source: Overall, online NREM sleep staging had a mean sensitivity of 12%, indicating how strictly the staging tool identifies sustained NREM sleep, and specificity of 98%, highlighting the high rejection rate of events in disagreement with NREM characteristics (Figure 3a, see detailed methods 'EEG/EMG offline scoring and online staging validation' section).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: 70% of epochs on average were confirmed offline as NREM sleep regarding online precision of NREM sleep staging.
source: Regarding online precision of NREM sleep staging, 70% of epochs on average were confirmed offline as NREM sleep, whereas 18% were later identified as wakefulness and 2% as REM sleep (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3b.

claim: Up-phase paradigm revealed M = 74.97° (SD = 38.10°; Var = 12.67°) while down-phase stimulation indicated a mean target M = 280.55° (SD = 49.67°; Var = 19.75°).
source: Up-phase paradigm revealed M = 74.97° (SD = 38.10°; Var = 12.67°) while down-phase stimulation indicated a mean target M = 280.55° (SD = 49.67°; Var = 19.75°).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as measured data.

claim: In mock animals, onset of muted triggers was confirmed around the positive peak of the slow wave (M = 101.20°; SD = 46.89°; Var = 19.19°).
source: In mock animals, we confirmed onset of muted triggers around the positive peak of the slow wave (M = 101.20°; SD = 46.89°; Var = 19.19°) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3c.

claim: Up-phase-stimulated animals received more sound triggers during NREM sleep than down-phase-stimulated subjects.
source: Additionally, we explored the distribution of triggers across sleep stages and observed that up-phase-stimulated animals received more sound triggers during NREM sleep than down-phase-stimulated subjects (up-phase: M = 4959, SD = 3063; down-phase: M = 3148, SD = 2719; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The proportion of triggers did not differ between stimulation groups for any of the sleep stages.
source: Nonetheless, the proportion of triggers did not differ between stimulation groups for any of the sleep stages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Neither up-phase nor down-phase stimulation disturbed total NREM amount compared to mock condition.
source: Neither up-phase nor down-phase stimulation disturbed total NREM amount compared to mock condition (two-way repeated measures analysis of variance [RM-ANOVA], time * condition interaction, F(32, 215) = 0.929, p=0.582, Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4a.

claim: No evidence of abnormal NREM sleep fragmentation was observed in any stimulation group over time.
source: Moreover, we observed no evidence of abnormal NREM sleep fragmentation in any stimulation group over time (RM-ANOVA, time * condition interaction, F(32, 228) = 0.830, p=0.730, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4b.

claim: On third day of motor training (M-T3), 24 hr EEG power spectra in NREM exhibited increased delta activity in the up-phase-stimulated group.
source: On third day of motor training (M-T3), 24 hr EEG power spectra in NREM exhibited increased delta activity in the up-phase-stimulated group (Figure 4c), whereas down-phase-stimulated animals showed a trend towards decreased delta-frequency activity (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4c.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated animals showed a trend towards decreased delta-frequency activity on M-T3.
source: On third day of motor training (M-T3), 24 hr EEG power spectra in NREM exhibited increased delta activity in the up-phase-stimulated group (Figure 4c), whereas down-phase-stimulated animals showed a trend towards decreased delta-frequency activity (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4e.

claim: Delta (***p<0.001), sigma (11–16 Hz, ***p<0.001), and beta (16–30 Hz, *p=0.045) bands were significantly increased in up-phase-stimulated subjects across the spectrum from P-T1 to M-T3 days.
source: Across the spectrum, delta (***p<0.001), sigma (11–16 Hz, ***p<0.001), and beta (16–30 Hz, *p=0.045) bands were significantly increased in up-phase-stimulated subjects.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical significance values.

claim: Down-phase stimulation decreased delta (***p<0.001), alpha (8–11 Hz, *p=0.037), and sigma (*p=0.012) power during P-T1 – M-T3 days, collectively.
source: On the contrary, down-phase stimulation decreased delta (***p<0.001), alpha (8–11 Hz, *p=0.037), and sigma (*p=0.012) power during P-T1 – M-T3 days, collectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical significance values.

claim: Mock animals showed altered power in the sigma band (**p=0.002), an apparent effect of the skill learning task performed daily.
source: Mock animals showed altered power in the sigma band (**p=0.002, one-sample Hotelling's T2, Figure 4f), an apparent effect of the skill learning task performed daily.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4f.

claim: Mock animals returned to BL indices during the N-T period (p=0.672) for sigma activity.
source: This effect was corroborated by examining sigma activity during the N-T period — 4 days without motor skill training — in all three groups: mock animals returned to BL indices (p=0.672), whereas up-phase (**p=0.002) and down-phase (*p=0.028)-stimulated groups showed increased and decreased sigma activity, respectively (one-sample t-test, Figure 4g).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4g.

claim: Up-phase (**p=0.002) and down-phase (*p=0.028)-stimulated groups showed increased and decreased sigma activity, respectively, during the N-T period.
source: This effect was corroborated by examining sigma activity during the N-T period — 4 days without motor skill training — in all three groups: mock animals returned to BL indices (p=0.672), whereas up-phase (**p=0.002) and down-phase (*p=0.028)-stimulated groups showed increased and decreased sigma activity, respectively (one-sample t-test, Figure 4g).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4g.

claim: Both up- and down-phase-stimulated animals presented relatively symmetrical spectral power during wakefulness, NREM sleep, and REM sleep on protocol day M-T3.
source: Evaluation of protocol day M-T3 showed that both up- and down-phase-stimulated animals presented relatively symmetrical spectral power during wakefulness, NREM sleep, and REM sleep (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f.

claim: Up-phase-stimulated animals consistently presented increased delta power throughout the day, with larger increases during the light phase (up to ~23% in some days).
source: Up-phase-stimulated animals consistently presented increased delta power throughout the day, with larger increases during the light phase (up to ~23% in some days), an effect that persisted until the end of the protocol (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5a.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated animals exhibited reduced delta power for the majority of the time, with greater hourly decreases during the dark period, down to ~–17%.
source: Down-phase-stimulated animals exhibited reduced delta power for the majority of the time, with greater hourly decreases during the dark period, down to ~–17% (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5c.

claim: In up-phase-stimulated animals, the time-course analysis of delta activity revealed significantly higher power during the hours immediately after the testing session compared to BL.
source: In up-phase-stimulated animals, the time-course analysis of delta activity revealed significantly higher power during the hours immediately after the testing session compared to BL (multiple paired t-tests, corrected with Holm–Sidak method for multiple comparisons; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 5d.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated animals presented the largest decrease compared to BL during the hours immediately before the SPRT.
source: While mock animals did not show differences during the aforementioned stimulation days compared to BL (Figure 5e), down-phase-stimulated animals presented the largest decrease compared to BL during the hours immediately before the SPRT (multiple paired t-tests, corrected with Holm–Sidak method for multiple comparisons; Figure 5f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 5f.

claim: Up-phase CLAS preserves the natural proportion of same-size trains of triggers, whereas down-phase CLAS prolongs the interval between triggers.
source: Up-phase CLAS preserves the natural proportion of same-size trains of triggers, whereas down-phase CLAS prolongs the interval between triggers
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Up-phase-stimulated animals showed no difference in proportion of trains of any size when compared to the mock group.
source: Up-phase-stimulated animals showed no difference in proportion of trains of any size when compared to the mock group (Figure 6a); however, they overall received more triggers per day (M = 5862, SD = 2214).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6a.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated subjects presented a different pattern of stimulation (two-way ANOVA, condition * train size interaction, F(8, 80) = 6.72, ***p<0.001).
source: Conversely, down-phase-stimulated subjects presented a different pattern of stimulation (two-way ANOVA, condition * train size interaction, F(8, 80) = 6.72, ***p<0.001, Figure 6a), with significant higher rate of single triggers (***p<0.001, ~58% of all triggers in NREM per 24 hr, M = 2462, SD = 1686) and less trains of two triggers (*p=0.020), hinting on the disruptive effects of down-phase targeting on slow waves.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 6a.

claim: Up-phase targeting preserved the proportion of same-length non-stimulated periods seen in the analysis of muted-sound triggers in non-stimulated subjects.
source: Corroborating these results, the analysis of ISIs (two-way ANOVA, condition * ISI interaction, F(16, 144) = 1.80, *p=0.037) showed that up-phase targeting preserved the proportion of same-length non-stimulated periods seen in the analysis of muted-sound triggers in non-stimulated subjects, whereas down-phase stimulation provided a distribution of triggers containing significantly less density of ISIs < 2 s (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 6b.

claim: Up-phase CLAS mildly entrains EEG slow waves, whereas stimulation during the down-phase disturbs it.
source: Up-phase CLAS mildly entrains EEG slow waves, whereas stimulation during the down-phase disturbs it
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of event-related potentials revealed a small slow-wave cycle following the endogenous cycle that triggered the stimulation in up-phase CLAS.
source: Analysis of event-related potentials (ERPs, filtered in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band), that is, all waveforms receiving triggers during NREM, revealed a small slow-wave cycle following the endogenous cycle that triggered the stimulation in up-phase CLAS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), while down-phase targeting appeared to completely disrupt the slow-wave negative half-cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Down-phase targeting appeared to completely disrupt the slow-wave negative half-cycle.
source: Analysis of event-related potentials (ERPs, filtered in the 0.5–2 Hz frequency band), that is, all waveforms receiving triggers during NREM, revealed a small slow-wave cycle following the endogenous cycle that triggered the stimulation in up-phase CLAS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), while down-phase targeting appeared to completely disrupt the slow-wave negative half-cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated subjects show significantly worse learning progression when contrasted with mock subjects (SR: Χ2(2, N = 21) = 17.50), ***p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparison up * mock: p=0.220, down * mock: *p=0.044).
source: Between-group comparison of success rate (SR, successes per total attempts) and fail rate (FR, fails per total attempts) demonstrated that down-phase-stimulated subjects present a significantly worse learning progression when contrasted with mock subjects (SR: Χ2(2, N = 21) = 17.50), ***p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparison up * mock: p=0.220, down * mock: *p=0.044, Figure 7b; FR: Χ2(2, N = 21) = 18.34, ***p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparison up * mock: p=0.155, down * mock: †p=0.056, Figure 7c.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 7b.

claim: Up-phase-stimulated animals show daily intra-session improvements, while down-phase-stimulated animals attempt less towards the end of the session.
source: Up-phase-stimulated animals show daily intra-session improvements, while down-phase-stimulated animals attempt less towards the end of the session
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated animals attempted significantly less towards the end of the session (first-bin * last-bin, *p=0.022) and significantly less than control animals during the last bin (down * mock, *p=0.037).
source: Compartmentalizing each training session into 12 min bins (or 20 pellets, whichever comes first) revealed that up-phase-stimulated and mock subjects maintained the same rate of attempted grasps across bins (RM-ANOVA, condition * bin interaction, F(2, 18) = 4.03, *p=0.036, Figure 8a), while down-phase-stimulated animals attempted significantly less towards the end of the session (first-bin * last-bin, *p=0.022) and significantly less than control animals during the last bin (down * mock, *p=0.037).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 8a.

claim: The magnitude of changes in the delta-frequency band was moderately correlated with the number of delivered stimuli, both for up- (Spearman's rho = 0.43, *p=0.022) and down-phase-stimulated animals (Spearman's rho = –0.41, *p=0.026).
source: To investigate whether the number of sound triggers influences the extent of delta power modulation, we extracted the number of triggers over each 24 hr period during the M-T phase for all stimulated animals. The magnitude of changes in the delta-frequency band was moderately correlated with the number of delivered stimuli, both for up- (Spearman's rho = 0.43, *p=0.022, Figure 9a) and down-phase-stimulated animals (Spearman's rho = –0.41, *p=0.026, Figure 9a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 9a.

claim: A significant positive association was found between 24 hr changes in delta and sigma power (Spearman's rho = 0.57, **p=0.004).
source: We also found a significant positive association between 24 hr changes in delta and sigma power (Spearman's rho = 0.57, **p=0.004, Figure 9b), reflecting the impact of CLAS on the two most dominant features during NREM sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 9b.

claim: Subsequent analysis between 24 hr average delta change (all training-phase days condensed) and SR at the end of the training phase revealed a moderate positive association between modulation of delta activity and SPRT performance (Spearman's rho = 0.41, *p=0.034).
source: Subsequent analysis between 24 hr average delta change (all training-phase days condensed) and SR at the end of the training phase revealed a moderate positive association between modulation of delta activity and SPRT performance (Spearman's rho = 0.41, *p=0.034, Figure 9c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 9c.

claim: Sigma activity changes positively correlate with SR scores (Spearman's rho = 0.53, *p=0.007).
source: Likewise, sigma activity changes positively correlate with SR scores (Spearman's rho = 0.53, *p=0.007, Figure 9d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 9d.

claim: This study observed a mild but specific average increase of 6.9% (up to 23% during the light period) in delta power per 24 hr on stimulation days compared to BL.
source: With this paradigm, we delivered auditory triggers to healthy rats continuously over a period of 16 days. We observed a mild but specific average increase of 6.9% (up to 23% during the light period) in delta power per 24 hr on stimulation days compared to BL.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: This effect was stable over the entire stimulation period evaluated, with no signs of decay nor facilitation effects over time.
source: This effect was stable over the entire stimulation period evaluated, with no signs of decay nor facilitation effects over time.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Reverse effects (M = –4.5%, down to –17.5% by the end of the dark period) were observed during down-phase stimulation.
source: Reverse effects (M = –4.5%, down to –17.5% by the end of the dark period) were observed during down-phase stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Application of CLAS in human subjects has often failed to demonstrate an overall inter-night effect (unperturbed night vs. stimulated night) of stimulation on power spectra.
source: Notably, application of CLAS in human subjects has often failed to demonstrate an overall inter-night effect (unperturbed night vs. stimulated night) of stimulation on power spectra (Papalambros et al., 2017; Papalambros et al., 2019), while comparison between same-night ON- and OFF-stimulation windows yielded significant stimulation effects that positively correlated with subsequent memory performance (Ong et al., 2016; Papalambros et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: This study provides first evidence of a long-term effect when comparing unperturbed 24 hr (BL) vs. stimulated 24 hr in a paradigm of continuous stimulation.
source: In this study, we provide first evidence of a long-term effect when comparing unperturbed 24 hr (BL) vs. stimulated 24 hr in a paradigm of continuous stimulation, somewhat challenging the proposition that the effect of CLAS is mediated by qualitative transient reorganization of SWA rather than of a general SWS or SWA enhancement (Papalambros et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key finding.

claim: Chronic sleep deprivation studies in rodents demonstrate a comparable effect, suggesting that strong homeostatic compensatory mechanisms may be at play.
source: Interestingly, chronic sleep deprivation studies in rodents demonstrate a comparable effect, suggesting that strong homeostatic compensatory mechanisms may be at play (Kim et al., 2020; Leemburg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The CLAS paradigm introduced here produces stable sleep modulation effects over time and successfully replicates the timing accuracy so far obtained in some methods of human CLAS.
source: Nonetheless, the CLAS paradigm introduced here produces stable sleep modulation effects over time and successfully replicates the timing accuracy so far obtained in some methods of human CLAS (Fattinger et al., 2019; Papalambros et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Like in humans studies, this study observed an additional modulatory effect of CLAS on power in the sigma-frequency band in rats.
source: Also like in humans studies (Henin et al., 2019; Krugliakova et al., 2020; Papalambros et al., 2017), we observed an additional modulatory effect of CLAS on power in the sigma-frequency band in rats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Sigma modulation was, just like CLAS-dependent delta changes, phase-target-specific and steady over the 16 days of stimulation.
source: Sigma modulation was, just like CLAS-dependent delta changes, phase-target-specific and steady over the 16 days of stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Down-phase-stimulated animals showed an increased number of single triggers, decreased proportion of trains of two triggers, and decreased density of <2 s ISIs, in contrast to maintained levels in the up-phase-stimulated group.
source: In comparison to mock, down-phase-stimulated animals showed an increased number of single triggers, decreased proportion of trains of two triggers, and decreased density of <2 s ISIs, in contrast to maintained levels in the up-phase-stimulated group, potentially indicating that down-phase CLAS has disarrayed the natural pattern of delta wave trains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Analysis of ERPs indicated the occurrence of a post-trigger slow wave when targeting 60°, whereas a post-trigger pattern disruption arises from 180° target stimulation.
source: In agreement with the apparent preservation of the slow-wave pattern with up-phase CLAS, and opposite effect with down-phase CLAS, analysis of ERPs indicated the occurrence of a post-trigger slow wave when targeting 60°, whereas a post-trigger pattern disruption arises from 180° target stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: CLAS of rodent slow waves may be altering the natural slow waves' pattern rather than significantly affecting their amplitude.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that CLAS of rodent slow waves may be altering the natural slow waves' pattern rather than significantly affecting their amplitude.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings.

claim: The mean delta activity change in motor-training days 1–4 in relation to BL correlated positively with SR on motor-training day 4 in the SPRT.
source: Moreover, we found that the mean delta activity change in motor-training days 1–4 in relation to BL correlated positively with SR on motor-training day 4 in the SPRT.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Delta activity changes during motor-training days 1–4 are actually driven by CLAS through the positive correlation found between the number of triggers and delta power changes in up- and down-phase groups.
source: Through the positive correlation found between the number of triggers—that is, extent of closed-loop auditory stimuli delivered—and delta power changes in up- and down-phase groups, we confirmed indeed that delta activity changes during motor-training days 1–4 are actually driven by CLAS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings.

claim: CLAS-dependent delta activity levels drive next-day performance in healthy rats.
source: Overall, these results suggest that CLAS-dependent delta activity levels drive next-day performance in healthy rats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings.

claim: The level of proficiency achieved at motor-training day 4 was maintained in all groups after 5 days without training.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the level of proficiency achieved at motor-training day 4 was maintained in all groups after 5 days without training.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: CLAS modulated sleep-dependent skill acquisition and retention only immediately following a motor-training session.
source: This observation suggests that CLAS modulated sleep-dependent skill acquisition and retention only immediately following a motor-training session.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings.

claim: Without prior active task engagement or performance saturation, up-phase CLAS per se seems insufficient to induce a significant performance enhancement at the present conditions.
source: In short, without prior active task engagement or performance saturation (Kvint et al., 2011), up-phase CLAS per se seems insufficient to induce a significant performance enhancement at the present conditions, whereas there was no evidence of skill decay induced by down-phase CLAS either.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings.

claim: There was no evidence of skill decay induced by down-phase CLAS.
source: In short, without prior active task engagement or performance saturation (Kvint et al., 2011), up-phase CLAS per se seems insufficient to induce a significant performance enhancement at the present conditions, whereas there was no evidence of skill decay induced by down-phase CLAS either.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Targeting slow waves with CLAS might have altered (up-: increased; down-: decreased) the normal recovery process after learning during wakefulness in rats.
source: Sleep-mediated synaptic downscaling, or recovery, after learning has been deemed critical to maintaining behavioral performance (Fattinger et al., 2017). Thus, it is conceivable that targeting slow waves with CLAS might have altered (up-: increased; down-: decreased) the normal recovery process after learning during wakefulness in our rats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculative explanation with a supporting citation.

claim: The number of attempts in the down-phase group seems lower than in the other groups at motor-training day 1, potentially indicating that before any memory consolidation process took place, these animals already performed worse than their counterparts did.
source: In support of this argument, we observed that the number of attempts in the down-phase group seems lower than in the other groups at motor-training day 1, potentially indicating that before any memory consolidation process took place, these animals already performed worse than their counterparts did.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation supporting a speculative explanation.

claim: Memory consolidation, a process at least partially mediated by spindles in which specific synapses are strengthened, is also potentially sensitive to CLAS.
source: On the other hand, memory consolidation, a process at least partially mediated by spindles (Diekelmann and Born, 2010) in which specific synapses are strengthened, is also potentially sensitive to CLAS (Krugliakova et al., 2020; Ngo et al., 2013a; Papalambros et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Positive correlations were observed between sigma—potentially a proxy for spindles—during motor-training days 1–4 and SR on motor-training day 4.
source: In fact, we did observe positive correlations between sigma—potentially a proxy for spindles (Holz et al., 2012)—during motor-training days 1–4 and SR on motor-training day 4.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The two theories (synaptic downscaling and memory consolidation) are certainly not mutually exclusive and sleep-dependent memory benefit could well complementarily rely on them both.
source: The two theories, however, are certainly not mutually exclusive (Klinzing et al., 2019; Wilckens et al., 2018) and sleep-dependent memory benefit could well complementarily rely on them both.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Distinct local network dynamics determined by paw dexterity may have potentially affected closed-loop stimulation features in an uncontrolled manner in left- or right-pawed experimental subjects.
source: Thus, as we solely tracked the left-hemisphere EEG derivation for CLAS, distinct local network dynamics determined by paw dexterity (Hanlon et al., 2009; Vyazovskiy and Tobler, 2008) may have potentially affected closed-loop stimulation features in an uncontrolled manner in left- or right-pawed experimental subjects and contributed synergistically or in opposition to the CLAS modulatory effects.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation with supporting citations.

claim: Animals in all groups present distinctively decreased delta power levels in the few hours before the behavioral test, likely attributable to food anticipation.
source: Lastly, in our temporal analysis of the delta power changes per 24 hr, we observed a clear pattern showing that animals in all groups present distinctively decreased delta power levels in the few hours before the behavioral test. Whether this activity pattern, likely attributable to food anticipation (Northeast et al., 2019), might have compounded with our CLAS-specific delta power findings remains to be determined and, ideally, further controlled in future experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation with a supporting citation.

claim: The broad range achieved by the phase-tracking algorithm might have contributed to the observed variable effects of CLAS across animals at the ERP level, ultimately leading to high interindividual variability on delta activity modulation.
source: Finally, in relation to the lack of effect of phase-targeted rodent CLAS on ERP amplitudes, as others demonstrated earlier, the broad range achieved by our phase-tracking algorithm might have contributed to the observed variable effects of CLAS across animals at the ERP level, ultimately leading to high interindividual variability on delta activity modulation, result that agrees with previous studies using non-adaptive prediction algorithms (Cox et al., 2014; Fattinger et al., 2017; Fattinger et al., 2019; Ngo et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation with supporting citations.

claim: This report presents the first successful implementation of phase-targeted CLAS in rats.
source: Altogether, our report presents the first successful implementation of phase-targeted CLAS in rats, demonstrating that phase-targeted continuous chronic CLAS is feasible, specific, and effective in rodents.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: Phase-targeted continuous chronic CLAS is feasible, specific, and effective in rodents.
source: Altogether, our report presents the first successful implementation of phase-targeted CLAS in rats, demonstrating that phase-targeted continuous chronic CLAS is feasible, specific, and effective in rodents.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: This novel tool provides successful grounds to not only further study the substrate mechanisms by which CLAS affects SWA and associated outcomes, such as cognition, but to additionally assess its effect on models of brains disease.
source: Overall, this novel tool provides successful grounds to not only further study the substrate mechanisms by which CLAS affects SWA and associated outcomes, such as cognition, but to additionally assess its effect on models of brains disease.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: CLAS of slow waves in rodents may help pave the way to the clinical implementation of this novel technique in the context of brain/body disorders that may be targeted with sleep-based therapeutics.
source: Ultimately, CLAS of slow waves in rodents may help pave the way to the clinical implementation of this novel technique in the context of brain/body disorders that may be targeted with sleep-based therapeutics (Arora and Taheri, 2015; Cook et al., 2020; Fung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion with supporting citations.

claim: 23 young adult male Sprague–Dawley rats weighing 200–220 g were used in this study.
source: To develop this tool, we used 23 young adult male Sprague–Dawley rats (Charles River, Italy) weighing 200–220 g and group-housed them in standard IVC cages (T2000) prior to interventions.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Electrodes for continuous recording of EEG/EMG were surgically implanted in all animals.
source: In all animals, we surgically implanted electrodes for continuous recording of EEG/EMG as described previously (Büchele et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: All procedures were approved by the veterinary office of the Canton Zurich (license ZH231/2015) and conducted in accordance with national and institutional regulations for care and use of laboratory animals.
source: All procedures were approved by the veterinary office of the Canton Zurich (license ZH231/2015) and conducted in accordance with national and institutional regulations for care and use of laboratory animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study opted to stimulate at 35 dB based on real-time video and posterior EEG/EMG inspection as none of the animals showed any perturbation during sustained NREM sleep under this volume.
source: We performed a series of small studies in a cohort of 10 animals (five animals under up-phase and five under down-phase CLAS) to investigate the most adequate set of stimulation parameters. Briefly, we opted to stimulate at 35 dB (range tested: 50 dB, 45 dB, 40 dB, and 35 dB) based on real-time video and posterior EEG/EMG inspection as none of the animals showed any perturbation during sustained NREM sleep under this volume.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 60° was selected for up-phase and 180° for down-phase stimulation based on literature and considering average delay from detection to trigger of 29.30 ms.
source: Based on literature (Fattinger et al., 2017; Ngo et al., 2013a), and considering average delay from detection to trigger of 29.30 ms, we selected 60° for up-phase and 180° for down-phase stimulation (we defined slow wave's 0° as the rising zero-crossing, 90° to the positive peak, and 270° to the slow-wave trough).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: 30 ms of stimulus duration was determined to overlap with the ongoing slow wave proportionally—slow oscillatory activity peaks at 1.35 Hz in rats.
source: Phase-target CLAS in humans typically uses 50 ms stimulus duration for a dominant slow oscillatory component of 0.8 Hz. Therefore, we determined 30 ms of stimulus duration to overlap with the ongoing slow wave proportionally—slow oscillatory activity peaks at 1.35 Hz in rats (Mölle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Differences between subjects contribute the most to the variability seen during closed-loop auditory stimulation (CLAS).
source: Differences between subjects contribute the most to the variability seen during closed-loop auditory stimulation (CLAS).
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 caption.
